source_text: Sic Chore et Dathan et Abiron, qui sibi contra Moysen et Aaron sacerdotem sacrificandi licentiam vindicare conati sunt, poenas pro suis statim conatibus pependerunt. Terra, compagibus ruptis, in profundum sinum patuit, stantes atque viventes recedentis soli hiatus absorbuit. Nec tantum eos qui auctores fuerant Dei indignantis ira percussit, sed et caeteros ducentos quinquaginta participes ejusdem furoris et comites, qui coagulati cum iisdem simul ad audaciam fuerant, exiens a Domino ignis properata ultione consumpsit, admonens scilicet et ostendens contra Deum fieri quidquid improbi fuerint ad destruendam ordinationem Dei humana voluntate conati. Sic et Ozias rex, cum thuribulum ferens, et contra legem Dei sacrificium sibi violenter assumens, resistente sibi Azaria sacerdote, obtemperare nollet et cedere, divina indignatione confusus et leprae varietate in fronte maculatus est, ea parte corporis notatus offenso Domino ubi signantur qui Dominum promerentur. Et filii Aaron, qui imposuerunt altari ignem alienum, quem non praeceperat Dominus, in conspectu statim Domini vindicatis extincti sunt.
pass_a_gloss: Thus Kore and Dathan and Abiron, who for themselves against Moses and Aaron the priest attempted to claim license for sacrificing, paid penalties for their attempts immediately. The earth, with its bonds broken, opened into a deep chasm, and the opening of the receding soil swallowed up those standing and living. Nor did God's indignation strike only those who were the authors, but also the other two hundred fifty sharers of the same fury and companions, who had been gathered together with them at the same time for boldness, a fire coming out from the Lord consumed them in swift vengeance, warning and showing that whatever things they had attempted in their wickedness to destroy God's ordination by human will is against God. Thus also King Ozias, when carrying the censer and violently taking to himself a sacrifice against God's law, with Azarias the priest resisting him, would not obey and yield, was confounded by divine indignation and was stained with a variety of leprosy on his forehead, marked on that part of the body where those who have earned the Lord are marked, because he had offended the Lord. And the sons of Aaron, who put strange fire on the altar, which the Lord had not commanded, were immediately extinguished in the sight of the Lord, avenged.

choices.why: refers to God's anger or wrath

pass_b_english:
Kore, Dathan, and Abiron tried to claim the right to sacrifice for themselves in defiance of Moses and the priest Aaron, and they immediately paid the penalty for their attempt (Numbers 16:1-35). The earth, its bonds broken, opened into a deep chasm, and the gash of the splitting ground swallowed them alive as they stood. God's indignation did not strike only the ringleaders; it also fell on the other two hundred fifty men who had shared their fury and joined them in the same act of rebellion. Fire came out from the Lord and consumed them in swift vengeance, warning and showing that whatever the wicked attempt in order to destroy God's ordination by human will is done against God (Numbers 16:1-35).

King Uzziah likewise took a censer and violently seized the sacrifice for himself contrary to God's law; when the priest Azariah resisted him, he refused to obey or yield. He was confounded by divine indignation and marked on his forehead with a disfiguring leprosy, branded on the very part of the body where those who have earned the Lord are marked, because he had offended the Lord (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). And the sons of Aaron, who put unauthorized fire on the altar, which the Lord had not commanded, were instantly struck down in the Lord's sight, avenged (Leviticus 10:1-2).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances (e.g., 'those who have earned the Lord' for 'qui Dominum promerentur'). Pass B provides appropriate biblical citations for the historical events described (Numbers 16, 2 Chronicles 26, Leviticus 10) which are alluded to in the Latin text. The title 'Punishments for Defying God's Order' correctly reflects the thought of the chapter.
